::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. info.title: Caught Between Two Worlds: The role of Bicultural Identity Conflict in the Longitudinal Effects of Perceived Discrimination on Migrants' Life Satisfaction and Health

text.text: Both forced and voluntary migration are incisive life events that prompt acculturation processes fundamental for the adaptation in the host society, including the formation of a second cultural identity.
One of the major challenges to the acculturation process is the discrimination by the host national groups.
Previous research showed that it can both undermine the development of integrated bicultural identities and impact migrants' well-being in many ways.
However, previous research investigating this process only relied on correlational methods.

Our study tests how dynamics between discrimination, bicultural identity, well-being, and health evolve over time, hypothesizing a longitudinal effect of discrimination on bicultural identity conflict as one important process that may link perceived discrimination with lower life satisfaction and health.
We conducted a secondary data analysis of longitudinal data with N = 285 migrants in integration courses in Germany (24,4% forced) including two time points spanning six months.

In two Latent Difference Score Longitudinal Mediation models we found that baseline perceived discrimination at time one predicted the increase in bicultural identity conflict over time, and that the increase in identity conflict covaried with a decline in (1) life satisfaction and (2) health.

The research highlights how the perception of discrimination can be a key risk factor that undermines the development of harmonious bicultural identity over time, with key detrimental repercussions for migrants' adaptation, life satisfaction and health.

Migrating to another country represents a major life event that entails acculturation processes (Berry, 1997; Schwartz et al., 2010) and prompts changes in one's cultural identity configuration (Ward & Szabò, 2023).

text.text: Migrants' intercultural encounters with the host national groups, ranging from positive interactions that support inclusion to negative experiences of exclusion and discrimination, have fundamental implications for fostering or constraining the development of dual cultural identities (Benet-Martínez & Haritatos, 2005).

text.text: These identity processes represent a central pathway linking intercultural experiences to migrants' adaptation and well-being, being associated with positive adaptation outcomes or psychological and physical burdens (Gonzalez-Guarda et al., 2021; Pascoe & Richman, 2009; Tikhonov et al., 2023).

text.text: When experiences of discrimination create tension between one's cultural heritage and newly developing national identity, people may feel emotionally burdened by these conflicting identities.
Over a longer period of time, experiences of discrimination and the entailing emotional identity processes might have profound effects on life satisfaction and health.

The implications of potential negative adaptations span multiple contexts, such as migrants' private lives as well as education settings and the workplace, and they affect both forced and voluntary migrants.

Drawing on longitudinal data we aim to test how the perception of discrimination can undermine over time the development of harmonious cultural identity, with ultimate detrimental repercussions for migrants' life satisfaction and health.
Migrants' integration hinges on how they negotiate their dual identification with both heritage and host cultures (Berry, 2001).

text.text: Models of acculturation suggest this can result in stable different identity configurations: prioritizing identification with one group, with both groups but alternatively depending on contextual factors, or integrating the two cultures into a blended and non-conflictual identity.

text.text: One major framework that describes individuals' subjective perceptions of how their multiple cultural identities relate to each other is the bicultural identity integration (BII) framework (Benet-Martínez & Haritatos, 2005; Ward & Szabò, 2023).
text.formatted: One major framework that describes individuals' subjective perceptions of how their multiple cultural identities relate to each other is the bicultural identity integration (BII) framework <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Benet-Martínez & Haritatos, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Ward & Szabò, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: It describes two independent dimensions of BIIperceived cultural conflict and perceived cultural distance.

Cultural conflict describes the degree to which a person perceives their relevant cultural identities as harmonious or conflicting, and cultural distance marks the perception of one's cultural identities as blended or compartmentalized.

In other words, the cultural distance dimension covers whether someone feels part of one combined culture (e.g. a hyphenated culture like Turkish-German) or keeps them separate (e.g. describing the self as a Turkish person living in Germany).
The cultural conflict dimension describes whether a person feels torn between the two cultures or perceives them as harmonious and compatible.

These two dimensions are distinct and are associated with different factors (Huynh et al., 2018), where, for example, perceived discrimination is explicitly associated primarily with cultural conflict, but not cultural distance.
text.formatted: These two dimensions are distinct and are associated with different factors <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Huynh et al., 2018</ref>), where, for example, perceived discrimination is explicitly associated primarily with cultural conflict, but not cultural distance.

text.text: Therefore, the present study centers the cultural conflict dimension with its particular focus on affective processes, especially in the light of experiences of discrimination and the resulting effects on life satisfaction and health.

This way, the BII can explain how a person might see their cultural identity as one that combines both national and heritage culture, but at the same time as conflicting: A migrant might happily celebrate a national holiday in their private life that is not part of their cultural heritage (i.e. low cultural distance), but at the same time feel distress from a cultural clash through discrimination experiences and intercultural tensions (i.e. high cultural conflict).

While the BII framework adds a more micro-level perspective on how individuals reconcile multiple cultural identities, the importance of migrants dual identities could be further understood in light of additional socio-psychological theoretical frameworks that focus on the main benefits of mere group identities (i.e., belonging to one or more social groups for ones' life satisfaction and health) and group-level identity continuity (i.e., finding compatible new groups after an incisive life transition).
The social cure approach (Haslam et al., 2018; Jetten et al., 2012) emphasizes the implications of social identities and their compatibility for health.

text.text: The approach supports that group identification can convey fundamental psychological resources like social support, need satisfaction, self-esteem, meaning, and adaptive regulatory strategies that sustain a healthy psycho-biological functioning with positive implications for life satisfaction and health.
A growing body of mostly cross-sectional research points out the effect of perceived discrimination on health outcomes (Cobb et al., 2019; Gonzalez-Guarda et al., 2021; Scholaske et al., 2021).

text.text: This evidence suggests the importance of considering health alongside life satisfaction to grasp a full picture of how dual identities could shape migrants' well-being outcomes.

Within the broader social cure approach, the Social Identity Model of Identity Change (SIMIC; Haslam et al., 2020) highlights the importance of multiple compatible old and new social group memberships following an incisive life event, such as migration.

text.text: Specifically, the SIMIC proposes that compatibility between group memberships before and after a significant life transition is necessary to maintain a sense of identity continuity, which in turn supports well-being during adjustment.
Indeed, a certain degree of identity continuity is an important psychosocial resource for well-being in such transitions (Haslam et al., 2020; Smeekes et al., 2017).

text.text: It ensures successful integration into new social groups, whereas incompatibility blocks social support, and thus, poses a risk factor for psychological burdens like depression (Haslam et al., 2020; Jetten et al., 2012).

text.text: The SIMIC and the BII framework converge in their assertion that compatibility is an important aspect of well-being and adaptation during life transitions.
Both accounts offer differentiated explanations of how exactly migration, discrimination, and internal identity processes shape well-being outcomes.
When considering both accounts, we can explain in more detail the experience of bicultural identities.

High identity continuity after migration (i.e., retained group memberships related to cultural heritage) might support well-being while at the same time, perceived discrimination might induce bicultural identity conflict that burdens well-being.

This way, discrimination might disrupt identity continuity in addition to causing bicultural identity conflict by blocking access to previously valued groups, potentially resulting in an exacerbated negative effect on well-being.

The importance of migrants' dual cultural identities extends beyond their direct effects on wellbeing and adaptation outcomes, as they may play a crucial role in shaping the psychological processes arising from one of the most challenging social experiences migrants face: exclusion and discrimination.
Meta-analyses strongly point out the negative effect of perceived discrimination on both life satisfaction and multiple health outcomes (Pascoe et al., 2009; Schmitt et al., 2014).

text.text: For migrants, perceived discrimination and exclusionary threat are among key detrimental acculturative stress factors that pose an additional burden to their well-being and struggle to integrate.

Social exclusion negatively affects psychological needs such as belonging and self-esteem (Marinucci & Riva, 2021a; Marinucci et al., 2022) leading to chronic feelings of psychological resignation (Marinucci & Riva, 2021b), that could ultimately play a role in marginalization processes (Berry, 1997).

text.text: The potential mediating role of bicultural identity conflict, however, has not been studied longitudinally, nor has it considered the possible implications for health.

Indeed, evidence of this effect is only preliminary and correlational, and it is not clear yet whether bicultural identity conflict can mediate the longitudinal impact of discrimination on both health and life satisfaction.

text.text: After removing participants who failed the attention check or declared they had not understood the questionnaire well, the final sample consisted of 285 migrants (40.8% women, 59.2% men) of 34 years old (SD = 9.1, range = 17-63).
Participants came from all over the world.

The majority originated from the Middle East (33.5%; e.g., Syria, Turkey, Iran), followed by East Europe and Russia (26.8%; e.g., Albania, Poland, Ukraine), South and East Asia (11.9%; e.g., India, Pakistan, Philippines), Central and South America (11.5%; e.g., Brazil, Venezuela, Colombia), Africa (9.1%; e.g., Tunisia, Nigeria, Somalia), and the Western World (7.2%; e.g., other European countries, USA, Australia).
Most of the participants were voluntary migrants (75.6%), moving to Germany for economic, study, or family reasons, whereas 24.4% were forced migrants (refugees and asylum seekers).
On average, participants had been staying in Germany for 2.3 years (SD = 2.6, range = 1-30).
Of the final sample, 165 participants completed the second wave of data collection after 6 months.
Participants were attending German integration courses in Berlin, North Rhine-Westphalia, and Munich as part of a project with Germany's Ministry for Migration.
Participants were recruited in person at the beginning of the courses.

Overall, there were three time-points: -At T0 (the time of recruitment in the course), we assessed demographic information in a brief in-person survey -At T1, approximately one month after t0, we assessed our variables in an online-survey -At T2, six months after t1, we again assessed our variables in a second online-survey.
The in-person recruitment procedure ensured participants were really migrants.
The questionnaires were available in seven different languages (Arabic, Farsi, French, Russian, Turkish, English, and German) to meet the participants' linguistic needs.
Translations were made by professional translators, using back-and-forth translation methods.
The questionnaire took ~30 minutes.
Participants were compensated with 10 euros for their time and commitment to the project.
Variables were assessed using a 6-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree,6 = strongly agree) unless otherwise specified.
Besides the following, the broad research project assessed additional variables that fell outside the scope of the current study.

text.text: For both models, the measurement part estimated whether perceived discrimination, bicultural identity conflict, and life satisfaction/health significantly changed over time (i.e., the latent Δ-scores) 3.
Then, the structural part estimated all direct effects and the two possible indirect effects.
The change in identity conflict was predicted by baseline perceived discrimination (a1) and its temporal change (a2).

The change in life satisfaction/perceived health was predicted by the change in identity conflict (b2), the change in discrimination (c2), as well as baseline identity conflict (b1) and discrimination (c1).
The paths b2 and c2 present a covariance, rather than a strict temporal prediction, given the two-wave nature of the data and should not be interpreted causally.
Two indirect effects were computed using a bootstrapping method to test significant mediations (Preacher & Hayes, 2004).
text.formatted: Two indirect effects were computed using a bootstrapping method to test significant mediations <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Preacher & Hayes, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: The first (a1b2) assessed whether baseline discrimination levels had a downstream impact on life satisfaction/health by fostering greater identity conflict.
The second (a2b2) captured the extent to which change in discrimination indirectly reduced life satisfaction via increased identity conflict over time.

Importantly, both the baseline level (T1) and the change score of the predictor and mediator were included as predictors of change in the mediator and outcome because baseline levels may reflect chronic, cumulative exposure, while change scores capture more immediate and dynamic shifts (McArdle, 2009).

text.text: Modeling both enables a more nuanced understanding of which between chronic vs. dynamic shifts in the experiences of discrimination/identity conflict are more strongly implicated in shaping identity-related distress and well-being over time.
The models were estimated with full-information maximum likelihood.

Models' fit was assessed with the Comparative Fit (CFI) and Tucker-Lewis Indexes (TLI) (acceptable above .90), the Root Mean Square Error of Approximation (RMSEA) (acceptable below .08), and the Standardized Root Mean Squared Residual (SRMR) (acceptable below .07) (Hu & Bentler, 1999; Marsh et al., 2005).

text.text: Model 1 had an excellent fit (χ 2 (6) = 8.67, p = .193; CFI = .990; TLI = .975; RMSEA = .040; SRMR = .046) and the measurement part highlighted that, on average, perceived discrimination remained stable over the two waves of data collection, identity conflict significantly decreased over time, whereas life satisfaction increased although the change was only marginally significant.
The structural part of the model showed that baseline, chronic experiences of discrimination predicted a significant increase in bicultural identity conflict over time.
In turn, the increase in identity conflict was associated with a decline in life satisfaction, potentially indicating a longitudinal mediation pathway.

Differently, neither the direct effects of baseline discrimination and identity conflict on the change in life satisfaction nor the change in discrimination on the change in identity conflict and life satisfaction were significant.

The analysis of the indirect effect suggests that the longitudinal effect of baseline perceived discrimination on the decline in life satisfaction was significantly mediated by an increase in bicultural identity conflict (a1*b2: β = -.053; 95%CI[-.123 -.003]), however, the second part of the indirect effect presents a covariance rather than a longitudinal prediction.
By contrast, the indirect effect involving the change in discrimination was not significant (a2*b2: β = .00; 95%CI[-.040 .043]).
Model 2 focusing on health largely showed the same effects.
The model had an excellent fit (χ 2 (6) = 9.14, p = .166; CFI = .987; TLI = .967; RMSEA = .043; SRMR = .047) and confirmed that only identity conflict changed over time, decreasing.

The structural part replicated model 1, showing that baseline perceived group discrimination led to an increase in identity conflict over time, which in turn, was associated with a decrease in perceived health, with the indirect effect being statistically significant (a1*b2: β = -.044; 95%CI[-.105 -.002]).
However, the second part of the indirect effect presents a covariance rather than a longitudinal prediction.
As in model 1, the effect of baseline identity conflict on the change in health was not significant.

Also, neither the effect of change in discrimination on change in identity, nor the indirect effect on change in health via change in identity conflict (a2*b2: β = .00; 95%CI[-.039 .032]) were statistically significant.

The only difference compared to model 1 is that the baseline effect of perceived discrimination significantly predicted an improvement in perceived health over time, and similarly, the change in discrimination predicted an increase in health (although only marginally significant).
These patterns indicate suppression effects (MacKinnon et al., 2000).
text.formatted: These patterns indicate suppression effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(MacKinnon et al., 2000)</ref>.

text.text: They imply that, net of the negative effect of discrimination on the decrease in health via identity conflict, the observed positive effect of perceived group discrimination on health may reflect the activation of compensatory coping mechanisms in response to discrimination, which may improve health outcomes.

Since the present study used a single-item measure of perceived discrimination, these findings cannot be attributed to specific kinds of discrimination, such as perceived group or personal discrimination.

The results of our study support the hypothesized mediation effect of bicultural identity conflict, with identity conflict mediating the relationship between perceived discrimination and life satisfaction as well as health: Baseline discrimination at time one predicted an increase in identity conflict at time two.
Across two models, the change in identity conflict was in turn associated with the change in life satisfaction and health, respectively, as predicted.
While the direct effect of baseline discrimination on life satisfaction was not significant, there was a significant positive direct effect of baseline discrimination on health.

Sensitivity analyses showed that the results hold the same across forced and voluntary migrants (see supplemental materials), suggesting that the found processes are not unique to forced migrants, highlighting the value of cross-migration comparisons.
The present study extends prior work in three main ways.
First, it contributes to clarifying the psychological pathways through which perceived discrimination erodes migrants' life satisfaction and health over time.

By focusing specifically on the BII's cultural conflict dimension, it sheds light on how perceived discrimination leads to an internalized identity struggle for migrants, a feeling of being torn between their heritage and their national identity.

It contributes to the literature on the sociocultural identitarian and psychosocial processes conveying the negative impact of perceived discrimination on migrants' life satisfaction and health.Second, inspired by the broader Social Cure Approach (Jetten et al., 2012; Haslam et al., 2018), which postulates that social identities are key determinants of not only psychological well-being but also physical health, the present study incorporates health outcomes alongside life satisfaction.

text.text: Within this theoretical framework, the present longitudinal study suggests that perceived discrimination led to negative life satisfaction and health consequences over time, potentially indirectly by increasing the perceived conflict between migrants' dual cultural identities.
This suggests that perceiving one's migrant national group as discriminated against can generate a lasting and hard-to-solve conflict within bicultural identity.

Being discriminated against by the host national group may signal that migrants' heritage national identity is not seen as fitting or compatible with the host national identity, thereby triggering enduring psychological feelings of being trapped between fixed features of who migrants are by heritage and who they are expected to become through adjustment.
Over time, this perceived incompatibility may undermine both health and life satisfaction.
Overall, the results suggest a nuanced pattern of temporal effects.

On the one hand, it was the chronic -rather than the change in -experience of discrimination that played a more central role in predicting bicultural identity conflict and its consequences for life satisfaction.

This suggests that the negative impact of chronic experiences of discrimination on inducing identity conflict might be persistent and not easily offset by short-term improvements in experienced discrimination.

On the other hand, it was the dynamic, short-term change in identity conflict rather than its chronic level that was associated more strongly with changes in life satisfaction, indicating that dynamic fluctuations in identity conflict might be a more proximal and immediate driver of life satisfaction than enduring levels of conflict.
The explanation is consistent with the differential temporal dynamics of the study variables.
Indeed, perceived discrimination remained stable over time, whereas bicultural identity conflict showed a significant decrease.

As such, the predictive power of chronic rather than changing discrimination likely reflects its stable nature, while the greater explanatory role of change in identity conflict may stem from its significant within-person fluctuations over time, making it a more transient and context-dependent psychological construct.

In the present study, we focus on a broad measure of perceived discrimination that does not distinguish group and personal discrimination, which might not catch all variation in different kinds of perceived discrimination over a period of six months.

Perceived group discrimination encompasses multiple contexts, such as work, housing markets, and institutions and surpasses individual instances, implying a more pervasive nature compared to perceived personal discrimination.
The non-significant change in perceived discrimination could also explain why the change score did not predict identity conflict over time.
Rather, our model shows that those with higher baseline level discrimination can, over time, experience an increase in identity conflict.
The results highlighting perceived discrimination as a stable temporal predictor align with other studies using related predictors, such as social exclusion.

They show the long-term negative effect of chronic social exclusion on migrants' and other marginalized groups' well-being (Aureli et al., 2020; Marinucci et al., 2022 Marinucci et al., , 2023;; Marinucci & Riva, 2021a , 2024).

text.text: Expanding the literature focusing on migrants' acculturation, cultural identity and life satisfaction (e.g., Ward & Szabò, 2023), the present research emphasizes that chronic experiences of discrimination may exert a stable and difficult-to-reverse negative impact also on identity-related processes, particularly on bicultural identity conflict.

text.text: However, its ultimate cascade negative impact on well-being might be interrupted and more easily targeted by leveraging fluctuations in bicultural identity conflict.

This highlights the potential value of interventions aimed at addressing and reducing identity conflict over time, suggesting that even in the face of persistent discrimination, fostering positive shifts in identity integration may offer a viable path to improving well-being.
The same reasoning applies also when considering perceived health as the ultimate outcome.

The only difference concerns a positive direct effect of baseline discrimination on health change, suggesting that in the absence of increased identity conflict, individuals high in perceived discrimination may mobilize compensatory resources (e.g., resilience, solidarity, identity affirmation) that positively impact well-being.

Specifically, after accounting for the negative effects of perceived discrimination on health via identity conflict, there was a residual positive longitudinal link between perceived discrimination and improvement of health.

The result pattern reflects a potential suppression effect, in which the mediating variable (identity conflict) accounts for the harmful pathway, thereby unmasking a residual positive effect of discrimination on health that might be explained by variables not considered in the current research -such as strengthening ingroup ties or the enactment of healthy coping mechanisms to face discrimination that would, in turn, benefit health.

This interpretation is consistent with the literature deriving from the Rejection-Identification Model (Branscombe et al., 1999), according to which perceived personal and group discrimination might lead minorities to strengthen their ingroup identity in order to cope with the enduring exclusion, as such unlocking beneficial effects for life satisfaction and health (Bourguignon et al., 2006).

text.text: Notably, the suppression-like pattern was observed only when the outcome was general health, not on life satisfaction.

This pattern might indicate that life satisfaction, as a more global evaluative construct, may be less influenced by coping strategies against discrimination, which might instead be more effective in improving specific health-related outcomes, like the reduction of physical stress (Pascoe & Richman, 2009).

text.text: Future research should clarify whether a suppression effect for health outcomes can be replicated in other samples or whether it is specific to the present research context.

Further work should also consider potential third variables that may account for the observed positive association between discrimination and improved health and explore why this effect appears to emerge specifically for health-related outcomes.
In this way, the present research also invites to consider possible coping mechanisms that could explain the positive link between perceived discrimination and improved health.
The found effect could serve as a starting point in research examining potential mediators.
For instance, future research could consider the role of other bicultural identity features, such as the blended integration of elements from both cultural identities.
Indeed, the current dataset did not assess this relevant feature of migrants' bicultural identity, which should be further investigated.

Similarly, it could be worth considering the psychosocial mechanisms proposed by the Social Cure approach (Haslam et al., 2018) -such as the strengthening of social ties and identification with ingroup members -which could unlock possible beneficial coping mechanisms against discrimination that would eventually protect well-being, such as health-promoting group norms.

text.text: It is important to note that the change scores in identity conflict and life satisfaction were both derived from the same two time points and thus refer to changes occurring over the same period.
As such, the path from change in identity conflict to change in life satisfaction should be interpreted more as a contemporaneous association than a strictly longitudinal prediction.

This limits causal inference regarding the direction of influence and suggests that identity-related distress and subjective wellbeing may co-vary over time, rather than one clearly driving the other.

As such, future research should consider conducting longitudinal studies with more than 2 waves of data collection, as to be able to conclusively identify the temporal chain of the effects between all the considered variables.

Research on migrants' acculturation experiences and identity processes in response to a new social and cultural environment is key to informing multiple stakeholders outside academia in social and workplace policy development on integration.
Specifically, our findings underline that bicultural identity conflict is a key process in BII.
Finding ways to foster BII amidst perceived discrimination could potentially buffer the negative effects of bicultural identity conflict on life satisfaction and health.
Reducing discrimination should be a primary goal, however, preventing all discrimination would still not be feasible, therefore calling for multiple simultaneous approaches.

It is both the behavior of individuals and groups, as well as institutional aspects that contribute to migrants' perception of discrimination against their own group (Marinucci et al., 2022), with detrimental effects on multiple outcomes, as found in the present study.

text.text: We argue that the prevention of discrimination and social exclusion and the resulting resignation in migrants is a central factor in the broader societal task of integration.

Further, in the context of discrimination, bicultural identity and well-being, both voluntary and forced migrants can be affected equally, highlighting the importance of a holistic approach to combating discrimination.
By including a diverse sample of migrants, we can highlight some crucial similarities in the psychological processes and outcomes following perceived discrimination.
Future research should address the potentially mediating coping mechanisms that migrants employ that could buffer the effects of discrimination on health.
